claims.text: A Pulumi package is the unit of versioning and distribution, and the components inside it inherit the package's version.
Pulumi recommends structuring Git repositories for publishing packages per the strategies in this guide (one package per repository, cohesive components).
Pulumi packages come in two flavors (source-based and executable-based), and each is versioned and released differently.
A source-based plugin package is distributed as source code in a Git repository.
The version of a source-based Pulumi package is the Git tag on its repository.

Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow (apply a semver Git tag, then run `pulumi package publish`), typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.
`pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.
The publish step in the source-based package flow often runs automated tests before publishing.
Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing source-based packages to the Private Registry.
Source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.

An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, the Go module proxy, or private equivalents).
The version of an executable-based Pulumi package is the version embedded in the published binary and SDKs.
Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
Executable-based package releases are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.
In both source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
A repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package, regardless of package type; this is Pulumi's recommended approach.
A repository containing multiple packages must either release them in lockstep or invent per-package release tooling that fights the way Pulumi naturally consumes packages.
A 1:1 repository-to-package mapping keeps git tags, release artifacts, and version history aligned.
Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are supported and expected, and the components ship together at the package's version.
The Amazon EKS package in the Pulumi Registry (at pulumi.com/registry/packages/eks/) bundles a managed Kubernetes cluster component along with supporting components needed to secure and operate it.
A single `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the repository root defines the package, with the components living alongside it.
It is technically possible to use a single monorepo containing one giant package for all of an organization's components, but Pulumi does not recommend it.
Semantic versioning is how consumers know whether a given change is a bug fix, a new feature, or a breaking change.
When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way, regardless of whether each component changed, which violates semver.

In a package with ComponentA and ComponentB, releasing v1.0.0, then an enhancement to ComponentA yields v1.1.0 and a breaking change to ComponentB yields v2.0.0, per semver rules (minor for feature, major for breaking change).
The Private Registry documentation is located at /docs/idp/concepts/private-registry/ and the `pulumi package publish` CLI reference at /docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_package_publish/.
A 'Publishing packages' page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/packages/publishing-packages/ covering publishing mechanics.
